chapters.title: Down the Rabbit-Hole
paragraphs: Alice was growing very tired of sitting beside her sister on the bank with nothing to do. Once or twice she had glanced at the book her sister was reading, but there were no pictures or conversations in it. “And what use is a book,” Alice thought, “without pictures or conversations?”

So she was trying to decide (as well as she could, since the heat made her feel sleepy and slow) whether making a daisy-chain would be enough fun to be worth getting up and picking the daisies, when a White Rabbit with pink eyes suddenly ran close past her.

There was nothing _so_ extraordinary about that. Alice did not even find it _particularly_ strange to hear the Rabbit say to itself, “Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!” (Thinking about it afterwards, she realised she ought to have been surprised; at the time, though, it all seemed perfectly natural.) But when the Rabbit actually _pulled a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket_, checked it, and hurried on, Alice jumped to her feet. It had struck her that she had never seen a rabbit with a waistcoat-pocket before, let alone a watch to pull out of it. Burning with curiosity, she raced after it across the field, and luckily arrived just in time to see it disappear down a large rabbit-hole beneath the hedge.
A moment later Alice went down after it, without once thinking about how on earth she would get out again.

For a while the rabbit-hole ran straight ahead like a tunnel. Then it plunged suddenly down—so suddenly that Alice had no time to think of stopping herself before she was falling down a very deep well.

Either the well was very deep or she was falling very slowly, because on the way down she had plenty of time to look around and wonder what would happen next. First she looked down, trying to see where she was heading, but it was too dark to make anything out. Then she looked at the sides of the well and saw cupboards and bookshelves all along them, with maps and pictures hanging from pegs here and there. As she passed a shelf, she took down a jar labelled “ORANGE MARMALADE”, but to her great disappointment it was empty. She did not want to drop it, in case she killed someone below, so she managed to put it into a cupboard as she fell past.

“Well!” Alice thought, “after a fall like this, tumbling down the stairs will seem like nothing! Everyone at home will think I’m so brave! Why, even if I fell from the roof of the house, I wouldn’t say a word about it!” (Which was very probably true.)

Down, down, down. Was this fall _never_ going to end? “I wonder how many miles I’ve fallen now?” she said out loud. “I must be somewhere near the centre of the earth by this time. Let me think: that would be four thousand miles down, I believe—” (You see, Alice had learnt several things like this in her schoolroom lessons. With no one there to listen, this was not a _particularly_ good chance to show off what she knew, but saying it over was still useful practice.) “—yes, that’s roughly the right distance—but what Latitude or Longitude have I reached, I wonder?” (Alice had no idea what Latitude meant, or Longitude either; she simply thought they were fine, grand words to say.)

After a little while she started again. “I wonder if I’ll fall all the way _through_ the earth! How funny it will be to come out among those people who walk with their heads pointing down! The Antipathies, I think—” (This time she was rather pleased that no one _was_ listening, because that did not sound at all like the right word.) “—but I’ll have to ask them the country’s name, you know. Please, Ma’am, is this New Zealand or Australia?” (She tried to curtsey as she spoke—imagine _curtseying_ while you’re falling through the air! Do you think you could do it?) “And she’ll think I’m such an ignorant little girl for asking! No, I mustn’t ask: perhaps I’ll see the name written somewhere.”

Down, down, down. With nothing else to do, Alice soon started talking again. “I should think Dinah will miss me terribly tonight!” (Dinah was the cat.) “I hope they remember her saucer of milk at teatime. My dear Dinah! I wish you were here with me! I’m afraid there aren’t any mice in the air, but you might catch a bat, and that’s much like a mouse, you know. But I wonder, do cats eat bats?” By now Alice was feeling rather sleepy. Dreamily, she kept repeating to herself, “Do cats eat bats? Do cats eat bats?” and sometimes, “Do bats eat cats?” Since she could not answer either question, you see, it hardly mattered which way round she said it. She felt herself drifting off, and had just begun dreaming that she was walking hand in hand with Dinah and asking her very seriously, “Now, Dinah, tell me the truth: did you ever eat a bat?” when suddenly—thump! thump!—she landed on a heap of sticks and dry leaves. The fall was over.

Alice was completely unhurt and sprang to her feet at once. She looked up, but overhead there was only darkness. In front of her stretched another long passage, and she could still see the White Rabbit hurrying along it. There was no time to lose: Alice raced away like the wind, just in time to hear it say, as it turned a corner, “Oh my ears and whiskers, how late it’s getting!” She was close behind when she rounded the corner herself, but the Rabbit had vanished. She was in a long, low hall, lit by a row of lamps hanging from the ceiling.

Doors lined every side of the hall, but all of them were locked. Alice went down one side and back along the other, trying each door; then she walked sadly down the middle, wondering how she would ever get out again.

Suddenly she found a little three-legged table made entirely of solid glass. Nothing stood on it except a tiny golden key, and Alice’s first thought was that it might fit one of the hall doors. But alas! either the locks were too big or the key was too small; whichever it was, it would not open a single one. On her second trip round, however, she noticed a low curtain she had missed before. Behind it was a little door about fifteen inches high. She tried the small golden key in its lock, and to her great delight it fitted!

Alice opened the door onto a tiny passage, scarcely bigger than a rat-hole. Kneeling down, she looked along it into the loveliest garden you ever saw. How she wanted to leave that dark hall and wander among the beds of bright flowers and the cool fountains! But she could not even get her head through the doorway. “And even if my head did fit,” poor Alice thought, “it wouldn’t be much use without my shoulders. Oh, I wish I could fold up like a telescope! I think I could do it if I only knew where to start.” You see, so many strange things had happened lately that Alice was beginning to think hardly anything was truly impossible.

Waiting beside the little door seemed pointless, so she returned to the table. She half hoped to find another key there, or at least a book of instructions for folding people up like telescopes. This time a little bottle was standing on it (“which certainly wasn’t here before,” Alice said). A paper label was tied round its neck, with “DRINK ME” beautifully printed in large letters.

Saying “Drink me” was all very well, but sensible little Alice was in no hurry to do _that_. “No, first I’ll check,” she said, “whether it says ‘_poison_’.” She had read several nice little stories about children getting burnt, eaten by wild beasts, and other unpleasant things, all because they _refused_ to remember the simple rules their friends had taught them: a red-hot poker will burn you if you hold it too long, for instance, and a _very_ deep cut in your finger usually bleeds. She had also never forgotten that drinking much from a bottle labelled “poison” was almost certain to disagree with you, sooner or later.

This bottle, however, did _not_ say “poison”, so Alice risked a taste. It was so delicious (a sort of mixture of cherry-tart, custard, pineapple, roast turkey, toffee, and hot buttered toast, in fact) that she soon drank the whole thing.
“What a strange feeling!” Alice said. “I must be folding up like a telescope.”

And that was exactly what was happening: she was now just ten inches tall. Her face lit up as she realised she was the right size to pass through the little door into that lovely garden. Before doing anything else, though, she waited a few minutes to see whether she would shrink any more. This worried her a little. “Because, you know,” Alice told herself, “it might end with me going out completely, like a candle. What would I be like then?” She tried to imagine what a candle’s flame looks like after the candle has been blown out, because she could not remember ever seeing such a thing.

After a while, when nothing else had happened, she decided to go straight into the garden. But poor Alice! At the door she discovered that she had forgotten the little golden key. She went back to the table, only to find that she could not possibly reach it. Through the glass she could see it perfectly clearly. She tried her hardest to climb one of the table legs, but it was too slippery. When she had worn herself out trying, the poor little thing sat down and cried.

“Come on, crying like that won’t help!” Alice told herself rather sharply. “My advice is to stop this minute!” She usually gave herself excellent advice (though she hardly ever took it), and sometimes scolded herself so fiercely that she brought tears to her own eyes. She remembered once trying to box her own ears for cheating in a game of croquet she was playing against herself: this unusual child was very fond of pretending to be two people. “But pretending to be two people is no use now!” poor Alice thought. “Why, there’s barely enough of me left to make _one_ respectable person!”

Before long she noticed a little glass box underneath the table. She opened it and found a tiny cake with “EAT ME” beautifully picked out in currants. “Well, I’ll eat it,” Alice said. “If it makes me bigger, I can reach the key; if it makes me smaller, I can crawl under the door. Either way, I’ll get into the garden, and I don’t mind which happens!”

She took a small bite and asked herself anxiously, “Which way? Which way?” With a hand on top of her head, she tried to feel which way she was growing. She was quite surprised to discover that she stayed exactly the same size. Of course, that is what generally happens when you eat cake; but Alice had grown so used to expecting only extraordinary things that life carrying on as usual seemed terribly dull and silly.
So she got to work and soon ate up the rest of the cake.

chapters.title: The Pool of Tears
paragraphs: “Curiouser and curiouser!” Alice cried (she was so astonished that she completely forgot, for a moment, how to speak proper English). “Now I’m stretching out like the biggest telescope there ever was! Goodbye, feet!” (Looking down at them, she could hardly see them any more, they were so far away.) “Oh, my poor little feet! Who’s going to put your shoes and stockings on for you now, my dears? _I_ certainly won’t be able to! I’ll be much too far away to bother with you; you’ll have to manage as best you can.—But I must treat them kindly,” Alice thought, “or perhaps they won’t take me where I want to go! Let me think: I’ll give them a new pair of boots each Christmas.”
She kept working out how to arrange it. “I’ll have to send them by carrier,” she thought. “How funny, sending presents to your own feet! And what a strange address it will be!

_Alice’s Right Foot, Esq., Hearthrug, near the Fender,_ (_with
     Alice’s love_).
Oh dear, I am talking such nonsense!”
At that moment her head hit the ceiling of the hall. She was now more than nine feet tall, in fact, and immediately picked up the little golden key and hurried towards the garden door.
Poor Alice! Even lying on her side, she could only just peer into the garden with one eye. Getting through the door was more hopeless than ever, and she sat down and started crying again.

“You should be ashamed of yourself,” Alice said, “a big girl like you” (and she had good reason to say that), “crying on and on like this! Stop it right now, I tell you!” But she kept on all the same, crying gallons of tears, until a large pool surrounded her. It was about four inches deep and stretched halfway along the hall.

After a while she heard tiny feet pattering in the distance, and quickly wiped her eyes to see what was approaching. The White Rabbit was coming back, magnificently dressed, carrying white kid gloves in one hand and a large fan in the other. He trotted along in a tremendous hurry, muttering, “Oh! the Duchess, the Duchess! Oh! won’t she be furious if I’ve kept her waiting!” Alice was desperate enough to ask anyone for help. As the Rabbit came close, she began in a small, frightened voice, “If you please, sir—” The Rabbit gave a violent start, dropped the white kid gloves and the fan, and fled into the darkness as fast as he could.

Alice picked up the gloves and fan. The hall was so hot that she kept fanning herself as she talked. “Dear, dear! Everything is so strange today! Yesterday it was all perfectly ordinary. Could I have been changed during the night? Let me think: was I still the same when I woke up this morning? I almost remember feeling a little different. But if I’m different, the next question is, who on earth am I? Ah, _that’s_ the really puzzling part!” She began going through all the children her own age that she knew, wondering whether she might have been changed into one of them.

“I certainly can’t be Ada,” she said. “Her hair hangs in such long ringlets, and mine has no ringlets at all. And I certainly can’t be Mabel: I know all sorts of things, and she—oh! she knows hardly anything! Besides, _she_ is herself, and _I_ am myself, and—oh dear, it’s all so confusing! I’ll see whether I still know what I used to know. Let me try: four times five is twelve, and four times six is thirteen, and four times seven is—oh dear! At this rate I’ll never reach twenty! But the Multiplication Table doesn’t matter: I’ll try Geography. London is the capital of Paris, and Paris is the capital of Rome, and Rome—no, I’m certain _that’s_ completely wrong! I must have been changed into Mabel! I’ll try reciting ‘_How doth the little_—’” She folded her hands in her lap as though reciting a lesson and began. But her voice sounded strange and hoarse, and the words came out differently from the way they used to:—

“How doth the little crocodile
    Improve his shining tail,
And pour the waters of the Nile
    On every golden scale!

“How cheerfully he seems to grin,
    How neatly spread his claws,
And welcome little fishes in
    With gently smiling jaws!”

“I’m certain those aren’t the right words,” poor Alice said. Tears filled her eyes again as she continued, “I must be Mabel after all! I’ll have to live in that cramped little house, with almost no toys to play with, and oh! so many lessons to learn! No, I’ve decided: if I’m Mabel, I’m staying down here! They can put their heads down and call ‘Come up again, dear!’ as much as they like. I’ll just look up and ask, ‘Who am I, then? Tell me that first. If I like being that person, I’ll come up; if I don’t, I’ll stay here until I’m somebody else.’ But, oh dear!” Alice cried, suddenly bursting into tears. “I do wish they _would_ put their heads down! I’m so _terribly_ tired of being here all alone!”

As she spoke, she looked at her hands and was astonished to find that she had slipped on one of the Rabbit’s small white kid gloves while talking. “How _could_ I have done that?” she wondered. “I must be getting smaller again.” She stood up and went to measure herself against the table. As far as she could tell, she was now about two feet tall and still shrinking fast. She soon realised that the fan in her hand was causing it and quickly dropped it—just in time to stop herself shrinking out of existence.

“That _was_ a close call!” Alice said. The sudden change had badly frightened her, but she was very glad still to exist. “And now, the garden!” She raced back to the little door as fast as possible, but alas! it had closed again, and the small golden key was lying on the glass table, just as before. “Now things are worse than ever,” the poor child thought. “I’ve never been as small as this before, never! It really is too bad, I say!”

As she spoke, her foot slipped, and the next moment—splash!—she was in salt water up to her chin. At first she thought she must somehow have fallen into the sea. “In that case I can take the railway home,” she told herself. (Alice had visited the seaside once in her life, and had concluded that anywhere along the English coast you would find bathing machines standing in the sea, children digging in the sand with wooden spades, a row of lodging houses, and a railway station behind them.) But she soon realised that she was floating in the pool of tears she had cried when she was nine feet tall.

“I wish I hadn’t cried so much!” Alice said, swimming about and trying to find a way out. “I suppose I’m going to be punished for it now, by drowning in my own tears! That certainly _will_ be a strange thing! But then, everything is strange today.”

At that moment she heard splashing a little way off in the pool and swam closer to see what it was. At first she supposed it was a walrus or a hippopotamus. Then she remembered how tiny she had become, and soon saw that it was just a mouse which had slipped in, as she had.

“Now, would speaking to this mouse do any good?” Alice wondered. “Everything down here is so unusual that it can probably talk. In any case, trying won’t hurt.” So she began: “O Mouse, do you know the way out of this pool? I am very tired of swimming about here, O Mouse!” (Alice assumed this was how you should address a mouse. She had never tried before, but she remembered reading in her brother’s Latin Grammar, “A mouse—of a mouse—to a mouse—a mouse—O mouse!”) The Mouse gave her a curious look and seemed to wink one of its little eyes at her, but said nothing.

“Perhaps it doesn’t know English,” Alice thought. “It may be a French mouse that came over with William the Conqueror.” (Despite all her knowledge of history, Alice had only a vague idea of how long ago anything had happened.) She tried again: “Où est ma chatte?” It was the first sentence in her French lesson-book. The Mouse suddenly leapt out of the water and seemed to tremble all over in terror. “Oh, I’m so sorry!” Alice cried quickly, worried that she had hurt the poor creature’s feelings. “I completely forgot you don’t like cats.”
“Don’t like cats!” the Mouse cried in a shrill, furious voice. “Would _you_ like cats if you were in my place?”

“Well, maybe not,” Alice said soothingly. “Please don’t be angry. Still, I wish I could show you our cat Dinah. I think you’d grow fond of cats if you could only see her. She’s such a sweet, quiet thing,” Alice continued, almost to herself, as she swam lazily round the pool. “She sits by the fire purring so nicely, licking her paws and washing her face. And she’s so lovely and soft to hold—and such a wonderful mouse-catcher—oh, I’m sorry!” Alice cried again. This time the Mouse was bristling from head to tail, and she felt sure she had really offended it. “We needn’t talk about her any more if you don’t want to.”

“We, indeed!” cried the Mouse, trembling to the very tip of his tail. “As though _I_ would discuss such a subject! My family has always _hated_ cats: nasty, low, vulgar creatures! Don’t mention that name to me again!”

“I certainly won’t!” Alice said, eager to change the conversation. “Do you—do you like—like dogs?” The Mouse gave no answer, so Alice went on enthusiastically. “There’s such a lovely little dog near our house that I’d like you to see! A little terrier with bright eyes and, oh, such long, curly brown hair! He fetches things when you throw them, and sits up and begs for his dinner, and does all sorts of other things—I can’t remember half of them. He belongs to a farmer, you know, who says he’s so useful he’s worth a hundred pounds! He says he kills all the rats and—oh dear!” Alice cried sadly. “I’m afraid I’ve offended it again!” The Mouse was swimming away as fast as it could, churning up the pool as it went.

So she called gently after it, “Dear Mouse! Please come back, and if you don’t like them, we won’t talk about cats or dogs at all!” Hearing that, the Mouse turned and swam slowly towards her. Its face was very pale (with anger, Alice thought). In a quiet, trembling voice it said, “Let’s get to the shore. Then I’ll tell you my story, and you’ll understand why I hate cats and dogs.”

It was certainly time to leave: the pool was filling up with birds and animals that had fallen in. There was a Duck, a Dodo, a Lory, an Eaglet, and several other strange creatures. With Alice leading, the whole group swam towards the shore.

chapters.title: A Caucus-Race and a Long Tale
paragraphs: The group that gathered on the bank was certainly an odd sight: the birds’ feathers were bedraggled, the animals’ fur stuck close to their bodies, and everyone was dripping wet, uncomfortable, and cross.

Naturally, the first thing to decide was how to get dry. They discussed it together, and within a few minutes Alice found it perfectly natural to talk freely with them, as though she had known them all her life. She even had a lengthy argument with the Lory. In the end it became sulky and would say nothing except, “I’m older than you, so I must know better.” Alice refused to accept that unless she knew its age, and since the Lory absolutely refused to give it, there was nothing more to say.

Finally the Mouse, who seemed to have some authority among them, called, “All of you, sit down and listen! _I’ll_ have you dry soon enough!” They immediately sat in a wide circle, with the Mouse at its centre. Alice watched it anxiously, certain that she would catch a dreadful cold unless she dried off very soon.

“Ahem!” The Mouse assumed an important air. “Is everyone ready? This is the driest thing I know. Silence all round, please! ‘William the Conqueror, whose cause was favoured by the pope, was soon submitted to by the English, who wanted leaders, and had been of late much accustomed to usurpation and conquest. Edwin and Morcar, the earls of Mercia and Northumbria—’”
“Ugh!” The Lory gave a shiver.
“Excuse me!” said the Mouse, politely enough, though it frowned. “Were you saying something?”
“Not me!” the Lory said quickly.

“I thought you were,” replied the Mouse. “—To continue. ‘Edwin and Morcar, the earls of Mercia and Northumbria, declared for him: and even Stigand, the patriotic archbishop of Canterbury, found it advisable—’”
“Found _what_?” asked the Duck.
“Found _it_,” answered the Mouse, rather irritably. “Surely you know what ‘it’ means.”
“When _I_ find something, I know perfectly well what ‘it’ means,” the Duck said. “It’s usually a worm or a frog. What I’m asking is, what did the archbishop find?”

Ignoring the question, the Mouse hurried on: “‘—found it advisable to go with Edgar Atheling to meet William and offer him the crown. William’s conduct at first was moderate. But the insolence of his Normans—’ And how are you doing now, my dear?” it asked, turning as it spoke towards Alice.
“Still just as wet,” Alice answered sadly. “It doesn’t seem to be drying me one bit.”
“In that case,” said the Dodo, solemnly standing up, “I propose that this meeting adjourn, so that we may immediately adopt more energetic remedies—”

“Speak English!” the Eaglet interrupted. “I don’t understand half of those long words. And what’s more, I don’t believe you understand them either!” It lowered its head to conceal a smile; some of the other birds could be heard giggling.
“What I meant to say,” the Dodo replied, sounding offended, “is that a Caucus-race would be the best way to dry us off.”
“What exactly _is_ a Caucus-race?” Alice asked. She was not especially eager to know, but the Dodo had stopped as though it expected _someone_ to speak, and nobody else seemed likely to say anything.
“Well,” the Dodo said, “doing it is the best explanation.” (You may want to try it yourself one winter’s day, so I shall explain how the Dodo went about it.)

First it marked a racecourse in something like a circle (“the precise shape isn’t important,” it said), then stationed the others at various points along it. Nobody called “One, two, three, and away!” Instead, they started running whenever they chose and stopped whenever they chose, which made it difficult to tell when the race had finished. But after they had run for roughly half an hour and were quite dry, the Dodo suddenly announced, “The race is over!” Everyone crowded round it, out of breath, demanding, “But who’s won?”

The Dodo needed a great deal of thought before it could answer. For a long time it sat with a finger against its forehead (the pose in which pictures usually show Shakespeare), while everyone else waited silently. At last it announced, “_Everybody_ has won, and all must have prizes.”
A whole chorus of voices asked, “But who’s going to give out the prizes?”
“Why, _her_, naturally,” the Dodo said, pointing a finger at Alice. At once everyone pressed round her, shouting over one another, “Prizes! Prizes!”

Alice had no idea what she ought to do. In desperation she reached into her pocket and brought out a box of comfits—little sugar sweets—which the salt water had luckily not reached. She distributed them as prizes, and there was exactly one for each of them.
“But you know, she needs a prize as well,” the Mouse pointed out.
“Naturally,” answered the Dodo with great seriousness. Turning towards Alice, he added, “What else is there in your pocket?”
“Just a thimble,” Alice answered sadly.
“Give it to me,” the Dodo said.

They all gathered round her again. With great ceremony the Dodo presented her with the thimble: “We respectfully ask you to accept this elegant thimble.” When this brief speech was finished, everybody cheered.

Alice found it all very ridiculous, but their faces were so serious that she dared not laugh. Unable to think of a reply, she simply bowed and accepted the thimble, making her own face as solemn as possible.

Next they ate the comfits. This brought considerable noise and confusion: the big birds complained they could not taste theirs, while the little ones choked and needed pats on the back. Eventually it was over, and they sat in a circle again and begged the Mouse to tell them more.
“You did promise me your story, you know,” Alice said, “and the reason you hate—C and D,” she added in a whisper, rather afraid of offending it again.
The Mouse turned towards Alice and sighed. “My tale is a long and sad one!”

“Your tail certainly _is_ long,” Alice said, gazing down at it in amazement. “But why do you say it’s sad?” She went on puzzling over this while the Mouse talked, so that the tale took something like this shape in her mind:—

“Fury said to a mouse, That he met in the house, ‘Let us both
         go to law: _I_ will prosecute _you_.—Come, I’ll take no
         denial; We must have a trial: For really this morning I’ve
         nothing to do.’ Said the mouse to the cur, ‘Such a trial, dear
         sir, With no jury or judge, would be wasting our breath.’
         ‘I’ll be judge, I’ll be jury,’ Said cunning old Fury: ‘I’ll
         try the whole cause, and condemn you to death.’”
“You’re not listening!” the Mouse told Alice sternly. “What are you thinking about?”
“I’m very sorry,” Alice replied humbly. “You’d reached the fifth bend, hadn’t you?”
“I had _not!_” the Mouse snapped, its voice sharp and furious.
“A knot!” Alice said, looking round anxiously, always eager to be useful. “Oh, please let me help you untie it!”
“I’ll do no such thing,” the Mouse answered, rising and walking off. “Talking such nonsense is an insult to me!”
“I didn’t mean to!” poor Alice pleaded. “But you do take offence so easily!”
In answer, the Mouse merely growled.
“Please come back! Finish your story!” Alice called after it. All the others joined in: “Yes, please do!” But the Mouse just shook its head impatiently and walked a little faster.

“What a shame it wouldn’t stay!” the Lory sighed, once it had completely disappeared. An old Crab seized the chance to tell her daughter, “Ah, my dear! Take this as a lesson never to lose _your_ temper!” “Be quiet, Ma!” the young Crab said rather sharply. “You’d try the patience of an oyster!”
“I do wish our Dinah were here!” Alice said aloud, to no one in particular. “She’d bring it back soon enough!”
“And who, if I may be so bold as to ask, is Dinah?” enquired the Lory.

Always happy to discuss her pet, Alice answered eagerly: “Dinah is our cat. You wouldn’t believe how good she is at catching mice! And oh, I wish you could watch her chasing birds! Why, she’ll eat a little bird as soon as look at it!”

These words caused a remarkable stir in the group. Several birds hurried away immediately. An elderly Magpie began wrapping itself up with great care, saying, “I really must go home; night air is bad for my throat!” A Canary called shakily to its children, “Come along, my dears! You should all have been in bed long ago!” With one excuse or another, everyone went away, and Alice was soon alone.

“I wish I hadn’t brought up Dinah!” she said sadly to herself. “No one down here seems to like her, and I’m sure she’s the best cat in the world! Oh, my darling Dinah! I wonder whether I’ll ever see you again!” Poor Alice began crying once more, feeling terribly lonely and miserable. Before long, though, she again heard little footsteps pattering in the distance. She looked up eagerly, half hoping that the Mouse had changed his mind and was returning to finish his story.

chapters.title: The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill
paragraphs: It was the White Rabbit, slowly trotting back and looking anxiously around as though searching for something it had lost. Alice heard it mutter, “The Duchess! The Duchess! Oh, my poor paws! Oh, my fur and whiskers! She’ll have me executed, as surely as ferrets are ferrets! Wherever _can_ I have dropped them?” Alice immediately guessed that it wanted the fan and white kid gloves. Kindly, she began searching for them too, but there was no sign of either. Everything seemed to have changed since her swim: the great hall, the glass table, and the little door had all disappeared.

Before long the Rabbit spotted Alice searching and shouted angrily, “Why, Mary Ann, what _are_ you doing out here? Run home immediately and bring me a fan and a pair of gloves! Hurry up!” Alice was so frightened that she ran at once in the direction it indicated, without attempting to explain its mistake.

“He thinks I’m his housemaid,” she told herself as she ran. “Won’t he be surprised when he discovers who I really am! Still, I’d better bring him his fan and gloves—if I can find them, that is.” Just then she reached a neat little house. A shining brass plate on the door was engraved “W. RABBIT”. She entered without knocking and hurried up the stairs, terribly afraid of meeting the real Mary Ann and being thrown out before she could find the gloves and fan.

“How strange,” Alice said to herself, “running errands for a rabbit! I suppose Dinah will be sending me on errands next!” She began imagining what might happen: “‘Miss Alice! Come here at once and get ready for your walk!’ ‘I’ll be there in a minute, nurse! First I must make sure the mouse can’t get out.’ Though I don’t think,” Alice continued, “they’d allow Dinah to stay in the house if she started ordering people around like that!”

By now she had reached a tidy little room with a table by the window. Just as she had hoped, there was a fan on it, along with two or three pairs of tiny white kid gloves. She picked up the fan and one pair of gloves, and was about to leave when she noticed a small bottle beside the mirror. This one had no “DRINK ME” label, but she uncorked it and lifted it to her lips anyway. “Whenever I eat or drink anything,” she told herself, “_something_ interesting is bound to happen, so I’ll see what this bottle does. I do hope it makes me big again. I really am tired of being such a tiny little thing!”

It certainly did, and far sooner than she expected. Before she had drunk half of it, her head was pushing against the ceiling and she had to bend over to avoid breaking her neck. She quickly set the bottle down. “That’s quite enough,” she told herself. “I hope I don’t grow any more—I already can’t fit through the door—I wish I hadn’t drunk so much!”

Alas! It was too late for that wish! She kept growing and growing, until she soon had to kneel on the floor. A minute later even that was impossible. She tried lying down, with one elbow against the door and her other arm curled round her head. Still she grew. As a last resort she stuck an arm through the window and a foot up the chimney. “Now there’s nothing more I can do, whatever happens,” she said to herself. “What _will_ happen to me?”

Luckily, the little magic bottle had now done all it was going to do, and Alice stopped growing. But she was still extremely uncomfortable, and there seemed no chance whatever of getting out of the room again. No wonder she was unhappy.

“Home was much nicer,” poor Alice thought. “I wasn’t forever getting bigger and smaller there, or being bossed about by rabbits and mice. I almost wish I’d never followed that rabbit-hole down—and yet—and yet—this is quite an interesting sort of life, you know! I do wonder what _can_ have happened to me! When I read fairy-tales, I used to imagine those things never really happened. Now here I am, right inside one! Someone ought to write a book about me, they really ought! When I’m grown up, I’ll write it myself—but I’m grown up already,” she added sadly. “At least there’s no room _here_ to grow up any further.”

“But does that mean,” Alice wondered, “I’ll _never_ be any older than I am now? In one way that would be comforting—never becoming an old woman—but then I’d always have lessons to learn! Oh, I wouldn’t like _that!_”
“Oh, Alice, how silly you are!” she replied to herself. “How could you do lessons in here? There’s barely space for _you_, never mind any schoolbooks!”
She continued in this way, arguing first for one side and then for the other, until it became quite a conversation. After a few minutes, though, a voice outside made her stop and listen.

“Mary Ann! Mary Ann!” the voice called. “Bring me my gloves at once!” Small feet pattered on the stairs. Alice knew the Rabbit was coming to find her, and she trembled so hard that the whole house shook. She had quite forgotten that she was about a thousand times bigger than the Rabbit now, with no reason at all to be afraid of it.

Soon the Rabbit reached the door and tried to push it open. But it opened inwards, and Alice’s elbow was firmly against it, so the attempt failed. She heard it say to itself, “Then I’ll go round and climb in through the window.”

“No, you _won’t!_” Alice thought. She waited until she believed she could hear the Rabbit directly below the window, then suddenly opened her hand wide and snatched at the air. She caught nothing, but heard a small scream, a fall, and glass smashing. From this she concluded that it might just have fallen into a glass cucumber-frame, or something similar.
Then she heard the Rabbit’s angry voice: “Pat! Pat! Where have you got to?” A voice she had never heard before answered, “Sure, I’m here! Digging for apples, yer honour!”
“Digging for apples, indeed!” the Rabbit snapped. “Come here! Help me out of _this!_” (More glass broke.)
“Now, Pat, tell me what that is in the window.”
“Sure, it’s an arm, yer honour!” (The word came out as “arrum.”)
“An arm, you fool! Who’s ever seen one that big? Why, it takes up the entire window!”
“Sure it does, yer honour, but that doesn’t stop it being an arm.”
“Well, whatever it is, it has no business there. Go and remove it!”

A long silence followed, broken only by occasional whispers that Alice could hear: “Sure, yer honour, I don’t like it at all, at all!” and “Do what I say, you coward!” Finally she spread her hand again and made another grab at the air. This time she heard _two_ little screams and still more breaking glass. “There must be an awful lot of cucumber-frames!” Alice thought. “Whatever will they try next! As for pulling me through the window, I only wish they _could!_ _I_ certainly don’t want to stay here a moment longer!”

For some time she waited without hearing anything else. At last came the rumble of small cartwheels, followed by many voices speaking at once. She could pick out: “Where’s the other ladder?—I only had to bring one; Bill’s bringing the other—Bill! Bring it over, lad!—Here, stand them against this corner—No, tie them together first; they’re not even half tall enough—Oh! They’ll do; don’t be so fussy—Bill! Here, take this rope—Will the roof hold?—Watch that loose slate—Oh, it’s falling! Look out below!” (A loud crash.) “Now, who did that?—Bill, I reckon—Who’s going down the chimney?—Not _me!_ _You_ go!—I certainly _won’t!_—Bill must go down—Here, Bill! The master says you’re to go down the chimney!”

“Oh! So Bill has to come down the chimney, does he?” Alice said to herself. “Shy, they do seem to leave everything to Bill! I wouldn’t change places with him for anything much. This fireplace is narrow, certainly, but I _think_ there’s room for a little kick!”

She pulled her foot as far down the chimney as possible and waited. Soon she heard a small animal—she could not tell what sort—scratching and scrambling just above her. “This is Bill,” she told herself, gave one sharp kick, and waited to find out what would happen.

First she heard everyone cry, “There goes Bill!” Then the Rabbit’s voice rang out: “You by the hedge, catch him!” Silence followed, then another muddle of voices: “Support his head—Give him brandy—Don’t choke him—What was it like, old fellow? What happened? Tell us the whole story!”

Finally a weak little squeaking voice spoke (“That must be Bill,” Alice thought): “Well, I hardly know—No more, thank ye; I’m better now—but I’m far too shaken to explain. All I know is, something flies at me like a Jack-in-the-box, and up I shoots like a sky-rocket!”
“You certainly did, old fellow!” the others agreed.
The Rabbit’s voice declared, “We’ll have to burn the house down!” Alice shouted as loudly as she could, “If you do that, I’ll set Dinah on you!”

Everything instantly fell silent. “I wonder what they _will_ try next!” Alice thought. “If they had any sense, they’d remove the roof.” A minute or two later, movement began again outside, and she heard the Rabbit say, “A barrowful will be enough to start with.”

“A barrowful of _what?_” Alice wondered. She was not left wondering long: the next moment a shower of little pebbles rattled through the window, some hitting her in the face. “I’ll put a stop to this,” she told herself, then shouted, “Don’t you dare do that again!” There was another complete silence.

To her surprise, Alice saw that the pebbles lying on the floor were turning into little cakes. A bright idea struck her. “Eating one of these cakes is sure to change my size _somehow_,” she thought. “It can’t possibly make me any bigger, so I suppose it must make me smaller.”

She swallowed a cake and was delighted to feel herself shrinking at once. The moment she could fit through the door, she ran out of the house. Quite a crowd of small birds and animals was waiting outside. In their midst was poor little Bill the Lizard, supported by two guinea-pigs who were giving him something from a bottle. As soon as Alice appeared, they all rushed at her. She ran away as fast as she could and soon reached safety in a thick wood.
“First of all,” Alice told herself, wandering through the wood, “I need to grow back to my proper size. Second, I need to find the way into that lovely garden. I think that’s the best plan.”

It certainly sounded like an excellent plan, neatly and simply arranged. There was just one difficulty: she had absolutely no idea how to begin. As she peered anxiously between the trees, a small, sharp bark directly above her made her look up in a hurry.

An enormous puppy gazed down at her with big, round eyes, tentatively stretching out a paw to touch her. “Poor little thing!” Alice said coaxingly, trying her best to whistle to it. All the while, though, she was terribly afraid it might be hungry. If it was, it would very likely eat her, however sweetly she spoke to it.

Almost without knowing what she was doing, she picked up a small stick and held it out. With a delighted yelp the puppy leapt into the air, all four paws off the ground, then rushed at the stick and pretended to savage it. Alice slipped behind a huge thistle to avoid being knocked over. The instant she emerged on the other side, the puppy charged at the stick again, tumbling head over heels in its eagerness to catch it. Thinking that this was very much like playing with a cart-horse, and expecting to be trampled at any moment, Alice ran round the thistle once more. Now the puppy began making little rushes at the stick, running a short way forward and a long way back each time, barking hoarsely throughout. At last it sat down some distance away, panting, its tongue hanging out and its great eyes half closed.
Alice decided this was a good moment to escape. She set off immediately and kept running until she was thoroughly tired and breathless, and the puppy’s bark sounded very faint in the distance.

“And yet it was such a dear little puppy!” Alice said. She leaned against a buttercup to rest and fanned herself with a leaf. “I’d have loved to teach it tricks, if—if only I’d been the right size! Oh dear! I nearly forgot I have to grow big again! Let me think—how _am_ I going to do that? I suppose I should eat or drink something. But the real question is, what?”

What, indeed? That was certainly the real question. Alice looked all around her at the flowers and the blades of grass, but nothing seemed the right thing to eat or drink in her situation. A large mushroom grew nearby, about as tall as she was. After looking underneath it, on both sides, and behind it, she thought she might as well look and find out what was on top.

Rising onto tiptoe, she peered over the mushroom’s edge and immediately met the eyes of a large blue caterpillar. It sat on top with folded arms, quietly smoking a long hookah and paying no attention whatever to her or to anything else.
